### medtech:grb_14 (row 39/84)

- **gold refs**: Article 51, Article 53, Article 55
- **base refs**: Article 51.1.a, Article 51.2, Article 25  (gold_dropped=2, loose=0.333)
- **branch refs**: Article 51.2, Article 53.1, Annex XI  (gold_dropped=1, loose=0.667)

**Base live answer:**

```
The pharma company's foundation model is a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk. Because its cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 floating-point operations, high-impact capabilities are presumed under Article 51(2), triggering the systemic risk classification in Article 51(1)(a). As a general-purpose AI model provider, the company bears the baseline obligations in Article 53(1): technical documentation of the model including its training and testing process and evaluation results, kept up to date for the AI Office and national competent authorities (Article 53(1)(a)); information and documentation made available to downstream providers who intend to integrate the model, containing at minimum the elements set out in Annex XII (Article 53(1)(b)); a copyright compliance policy addressing reservation of rights under Union copyright law (Article 53(1)(c)); and a publicly available summary of the content used for training, following the AI Office template (Article 53(1)(d)). The open-source carve-out in Article 53(2) does not apply once systemic risk is established, so all four obligations apply regardless of how the model is licensed. On top of those baseline duties, Article 55 imposes four additional obligations specific to systemic risk: model evaluation using standardised protocols and adversarial testing to identify and mitigate systemic risks; assessment and mitigation of possible systemic risks at Union level that may stem from development, market placement or use of the model; tracking, documenting and reporting serious incidents and possible corrective measures to the AI Office without undue delay; and ensuring an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure. The company may rely on codes of practice under Article 56 to demonstrate compliance with both Article 53 and Article 55 obligations until a harmonised standard is published. The company must also ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among staff and other persons dealing with the model's operation and use, to the best extent possible, under Article 4. The general-purpose AI model regime runs parallel to the high-risk tier rather than inside it, so the Chapter III Section 2 requirements for high-risk AI systems do not apply to the model itself as a general-purpose AI model, though a downstream provider who integrates it into a high-risk AI system may become subject to those requirements under Article 25. Chapter V obligations, including Articles 53 and 55, apply from 2 August 2025 under Article 113(3)(b).
```

As a general-purpose AI model provider, the pharma company must maintain technical documentation per Annex XI, supply downstream providers with the information set out in Annex XII, implement a copyright compliance policy, and publish a sufficiently detailed summary of training data content, all under Article 53(1). Because the systemic risk threshold is met, Article 55(1) adds four further obligations on top of Article 53: model evaluation using standardised protocols including adversarial testing to identify and mitigate systemic risks (Article 55(1)(a)), assessment and mitigation of possible systemic risks at Union level including their sources (Article 55(1)(b)), tracking, documenting and reporting serious incidents and possible corrective measures without undue delay to the AI Office (Article 55(1)(c)), and ensuring an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for both the model and its physical infrastructure (Article 55(1)(d)). The provider may rely on codes of practice under Article 56 to demonstrate compliance with both Article 53 and Article 55 obligations until a harmonised standard is published. The Commission's General-Purpose AI Guidelines of 18 July 2025 address the compute thresholds and the one-third fine-tune rule for downstream modifiers, but those are Commission guidance rather than text of the Regulation. Confidentiality of information and data obtained by the AI Office and other authorities in the course of applying these obligations is governed by Article 78.
```

### graphrag:med_7 (row 41/84)

- **gold refs**: Article 11, Article 18, Annex IV
- **base refs**: Article 11, Annex IV  (gold_dropped=1, loose=0.667)
- **branch refs**: Article 11, Annex IV  (gold_dropped=1, loose=0.667)

**Base live answer:**

```
Article 11 requires the provider to draw up technical documentation before placing the high-risk AI system on the market and to keep it up to date, with the documentation demonstrating compliance with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements and providing national competent authorities and notified bodies with the information needed to assess that compliance. The minimum content is set out in Annex IV and covers: a general description of the system including its intended purpose, provider name, version, hardware on which it is intended to run, software and firmware requirements, forms of placement on the market, and a description of the user interface provided to the deployer; detailed information on the system's capabilities and limitations, foreseeable unintended outcomes and sources of risk, human oversight measures, and input data specifications; a description of the appropriateness of the performance metrics; a detailed description of the risk management system; a description of relevant changes made through the system's lifecycle; a list of harmonised standards applied or, where none, a description of the solutions adopted to meet the requirements; a copy of the EU declaration of conformity; and a detailed description of the post-market monitoring system including the post-market monitoring plan. Where the pharmaceutical company is an SME or start-up, it may provide the Annex IV elements in a simplified manner using the form established by the Commission, and notified bodies must accept that form for conformity assessment purposes.
```

### medtech:grb_22 (row 42/84)

- **gold refs**: Article 6, Annex III
- **base refs**: Article 6.2, Article 6.3, Annex III.5  (gold_dropped=0, loose=1.000)
- **branch refs**: Article 6.2, Article 6.3, Annex III.5  (gold_dropped=0, loose=1.000)

**Base live answer:**

```
An AI system used for risk assessment and pricing in relation to natural persons in the case of life and health insurance is high-risk under Annex III(5)(c), which Article 6(2) classifies as high-risk. The Article 6(3) derogation is available in principle, but only where the system does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights and performs one of four tasks: a narrow procedural task, improving the result of a previously completed human activity, detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing a previously completed human assessment, or a preparatory task. A system that profiles natural persons is always high-risk regardless of those conditions. A provider relying on the derogation must document its assessment before placing the system on the market and register the system under Article 49(2).
```

**Branch live answer:**

```
An AI system used for risk assessment and pricing in relation to natural persons in the case of life and health insurance is high-risk. Annex III(5)(c) expressly lists such systems as a high-risk use case, and Article 6(2) classifies any system falling within Annex III as high-risk. The Article 6(3) derogation does not apply where the system performs profiling of natural persons, which a risk assessment and pricing system of this kind inherently does; such a system is therefore always high-risk regardless of whether it otherwise meets one of the four derogation conditions. The provider must register the system in the EU database before placing it on the market, as required by Article 49(1) for high-risk systems listed in Annex III.
```

### expert_review:xr_13 (row 43/84)

- **gold refs**: Article 5, Article 6, Annex I, Article 50
- **base refs**: Annex I, Annex III, Article 6.1, Article 6.2, Article 5, Article 50.1  (gold_dropped=0, loose=1.000)
- **branch refs**: Annex I, Annex III, Article 6.1, Article 6.2, Article 5.1, Article 50  (gold_dropped=0, loose=1.000)

**Base live answer:**

```
An AI system that transcribes doctor-patient conversations is not prohibited and is high-risk only where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a medical device required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, which includes the Medical Devices Regulation and the In Vitro Diagnostic Medical Devices Regulation, satisfying both conditions of Article 6(1). None of the eight prohibited practices in Article 5 covers transcription of clinical conversations: the system does not deploy subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques, does not exploit vulnerabilities, does not perform social scoring, does not scrape facial images, does not infer emotions in the workplace or an education institution, does not perform biometric categorisation to deduce protected characteristics, and does not conduct real-time remote biometric identification for law enforcement. A pure transcription function is also not listed among the Annex III use cases, so the Article 6(2) route to high-risk classification does not apply on the basis of intended purpose alone. Where the system does not meet the Article 6(1) conditions, it is limited risk, and the provider must ensure that patients who interact with it directly are informed they are interacting with an AI system, under Article 50(1).
```

**Branch live answer:**

```
An AI system that transcribes doctor-patient conversations is not prohibited and is high-risk only where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a medical device required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, which includes the Medical Devices Regulation and the In Vitro Diagnostic Medical Devices Regulation, pursuant to Article 6(1). None of the eight prohibited practices in Article 5(1) reaches a transcription system: it does not deploy subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques, exploit vulnerabilities, perform social scoring, scrape facial images, infer emotions in the workplace or an education institution, conduct biometric categorisation to deduce protected characteristics, or perform real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement. A transcription system is also not listed among the Annex III use cases that Article 6(2) classifies as high-risk, because it does not evaluate eligibility for public assistance, assess creditworthiness or insurance risk, triage emergency patients, or perform any law-enforcement function. Where the system interacts directly with patients, the provider must design it so those patients are informed they are interacting with an AI system, under Article 50(1).
```

### graphrag:ng_10 (row 44/84)

- **gold refs**: Article 10, Article 15
- **base refs**: Article 10, Article 55.1.a, Article 9.1, Article 53.1.a, Article 56  (gold_dropped=1, loose=0.500)
- **branch refs**: Article 11, Article 10.2.f, Article 10.5, Annex IV, Article 9  (gold_dropped=1, loose=0.500)

**Base live answer:**

```
For a high-risk AI system, Article 10(2)(f) requires that training, validation and testing datasets be examined for possible biases likely to affect health and safety, have a negative impact on fundamental rights, or lead to discrimination, and Article 10(3) requires those datasets to be relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose. Where bias detection and correction cannot be achieved through other data, Article 10(5) permits processing of special categories of personal data subject to strict conditions, including a requirement that the records of processing activities state the reasons why such processing was strictly necessary and why the objective could not be achieved by processing other data. The risk management system required by Article 9(1) must itself be established, implemented, documented and maintained, meaning that the mitigation measures adopted in response to identified risks, including bias-related risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, must form part of that documented iterative process. For a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk, Article 55(1)(a) separately requires the provider to conduct and document adversarial testing with a view to identifying and mitigating systemic risks, and Article 53(1)(a) requires the provider to draw up and keep up to date technical documentation covering the training and testing process and the results of its evaluation, with Article 56 codes of practice available as a means to demonstrate compliance until a harmonised standard is published.
```

**Branch live answer:**

```
For a high-risk AI system, bias mitigation documentation requirements arise across three interlocking obligations. Article 10(2)(f) requires that training, validation and testing datasets be subject to data governance practices that include examination for possible biases likely to affect health and safety, have a negative impact on fundamental rights, or lead to discrimination. Where bias detection and correction cannot be achieved with other data, Article 10(5) permits the processing of special categories of personal data under strict conditions, including technical limitations on re-use, security and privacy-preserving measures, deletion once bias is corrected, and documentation of the reasons why such processing was strictly necessary. The technical documentation drawn up before placement on the market under Article 11, with content specified in Annex IV, must record the data requirements and training methodologies including data cleaning methodologies and methods to detect identifiable biases, the validation and testing procedures including metrics used to measure accuracy and potentially discriminatory impacts, and the design specifications including key design choices and assumptions made with regard to persons or groups of persons for whom the system is intended. The risk management system required by Article 9 must be documented and maintained throughout the lifecycle, and must include the identification and analysis of foreseeable risks to fundamental rights, the adoption of targeted mitigation measures, and testing to confirm those measures are effective.
```

### medtech:grb_02 (row 45/84)

- **gold refs**: Article 50
- **base refs**: Article 50.1, Article 50.2  (gold_dropped=0, loose=1.000)
- **branch refs**: Article 50.2, Article 50.1  (gold_dropped=0, loose=1.000)

**Base live answer:**

```
Article 50(1) is the operative provision. The provider of a patient-facing medical chatbot must design and develop the system so that the natural person is informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious from the point of view of a natural person who is reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect, taking into account the circumstances and context of use. Where the chatbot also generates synthetic audio, image, video or text output, Article 50(2) requires the provider to mark those outputs in a machine-readable format as artificially generated or manipulated.
```

```
For high-risk AI systems the applicable penalty ceiling is set by Article 99(4): administrative fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or, for an undertaking, up to 3 % of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, for non-compliance with the obligations on providers, deployers, importers and distributors (every obligation other than the Article 5 prohibitions, which carry the higher Article 99(3) ceiling of EUR 35 000 000 or 7 %). Under Article 99(6), for SMEs and start-ups each fine is capped at the lower of the percentage or the fixed amount. Penalties must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive.
```

**Base live answer:**

```
Yes. An AI system intended as a safety component of a robotic surgical device is high-risk under Article 6(1) because a surgical robot is a Class IIb or Class III medical device requiring notified-body conformity assessment under Article 43. Since the AI operates in a real-time control loop, Article 14 requires robust human oversight measures to allow the surgeon to override or reverse decisions. Under Article 72 and Article 73, the provider must establish post-market monitoring and report serious incidents, coordinating with the Medical Device Regulation Article 83 for layered surveillance.
```

### medtech:grb_08 (row 48/84)

- **gold refs**: Article 16, Article 9, Article 43
- **base refs**: Article 16, Article 43.3, Article 8, Article 9, Article 13, Annex III, Article 47  (gold_dropped=0, loose=1.000)
- **branch refs**: Article 6.1, Article 16, Article 43, Article 9, Article 13, Article 47, Article 48  (gold_dropped=0, loose=1.000)

**Base live answer:**

```
Before placing a high-risk AI medical diagnostic system on the market, the provider must satisfy the full set of Chapter III Section 2 requirements and the pre-market procedural obligations that Article 16 collects into a single duty list. On the substantive side, the provider must establish, implement, document and maintain a risk management system covering identification, estimation and evaluation of risks across the system's lifecycle (Article 9); apply data governance ensuring that training, validation and testing datasets are relevant, sufficiently representative and, to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete (Article 10); draw up technical documentation before market placement, with content meeting Annex IV, demonstrating conformity with all Section 2 requirements (Article 11); ensure the system technically allows automatic logging of events relevant to risk identification and post-market monitoring (Article 12); design the system so its operation is sufficiently transparent to deployers and accompanied by instructions for use covering capabilities, limitations, accuracy metrics and human oversight measures (Article 13); build in human oversight measures enabling assigned persons to understand the system's capacities and limitations, remain aware of automation bias, correctly interpret outputs, and intervene or stop the system (Article 14); and achieve appropriate levels of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity throughout the lifecycle, with accuracy metrics declared in the instructions for use (Article 15). On the governance and procedural side, the provider must operate a quality management system covering regulatory compliance strategy, design verification, examination and test procedures, post-market monitoring and incident-reporting workflows (Article 17); undergo conformity assessment before market placement, which for an Annex III system follows the internal control procedure in Annex VI unless harmonised standards are absent or only partly applied, in which case notified-body involvement is required (Article 43); draw up a written, signed and dated EU declaration of conformity (Article 47); affix the CE marking to the system or its packaging or accompanying documentation (Article 48); register the system in the EU database before placing it on the market (Article 49); and establish a post-market monitoring system proportionate to the nature and risks of the system (Article 72). Where the system also qualifies as a medical device subject to Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, Article 8 permits the provider to integrate the testing, reporting and documentation required under Section 2 into the documentation already required under that legislation, and Article 43(3) applies so that the Chapter III Section 2 requirements form part of that legislation's own conformity assessment procedure.
```

**Branch live answer:**

```
A medical diagnostic AI system that is itself a medical device, or a safety component of one, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I and required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation is high-risk under Article 6(1). Before placing it on the market, the provider must satisfy the full set of Chapter III Section 2 requirements and the pre-market procedural obligations set out in Article 16. On the substantive requirements, the provider must establish, implement, document and maintain a risk management system across the system's lifecycle (Article 9), develop the system on training, validation and testing datasets that are relevant, sufficiently representative and, to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete (Article 10), draw up technical documentation before market placement demonstrating conformity with all Section 2 requirements, with content as specified in Annex IV (Article 11), ensure the system technically allows automatic recording of events over its lifetime to enable traceability and post-market monitoring (Article 12), design the system so its operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret its output and use it appropriately, accompanied by instructions for use covering the matters listed in Article 13, build in human oversight measures enabling assigned persons to understand the system's capacities and limitations, detect anomalies, correctly interpret outputs, and intervene or stop the system (Article 14), and achieve appropriate levels of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity consistently across the lifecycle (Article 15). On governance and quality, the provider must operate a quality management system covering regulatory compliance strategy, design verification, examination and test procedures, post-market monitoring and incident-reporting workflows (Article 17), and establish a post-market monitoring system proportionate to the nature and risks of the system (Article 72). On the pre-market procedural steps, the provider must complete the conformity assessment procedure under Article 43, which for a system covered by the Annex I Section A medical device legislation runs through that legislation's own notified-body route with the Section 2 requirements forming part of that assessment. The provider must then draw up a written, machine-readable, signed and dated EU declaration of conformity containing the information in Annex V (Article 47), affix the CE marking visibly, legibly and indelibly to the system or its packaging or accompanying documentation (Article 48), and register the system in the EU database before placing it on the market (Article 49).
```

```
High-risk, where two cumulative conditions are met: the software is a safety component of, or is itself, a medical device covered by Regulation (EU) 2017/745 listed in Annex I, and that device is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under that regulation, per Article 6(1). Where those conditions are satisfied, the provider must follow the conformity assessment procedure prescribed by Regulation (EU) 2017/745, with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements forming part of that assessment and notified-body involvement applying where that sectoral legislation requires it, per Article 43(3).
```

**Branch live answer:**

```
High-risk, where two cumulative conditions are met: the software is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that legislation, per Article 6(1). Medical device software of this kind falls within Annex I, which lists Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices, so the deciding condition is whether the device classification under that regulation triggers mandatory third-party conformity assessment. Where that condition is satisfied, the provider must follow the conformity assessment procedure required by the applicable sectoral legislation, with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements forming part of that assessment, per Article 43(3).
```

### medtech:grb_20 (row 51/84) 🚫

- **gold refs**: Article 6, Article 9, Article 43, Annex III
- **base refs**: Article 6, Article 9, Article 16, Article 13, Article 49.1, Article 22  (gold_dropped=2, loose=0.500)
- **branch refs**: Article 6, Article 25.1, Article 25.4, Article 47, Article 71, Article 49.1, Annex V  (gold_dropped=3, loose=0.250)

**Base live answer:**

```
An oncology treatment-recommendation tool that advises on clinical regimens is high-risk under Article 6(2) read with Annex III(5)(a), because it evaluates eligibility for or access to healthcare services by or on behalf of a public authority, or, where deployed independently, it may qualify under the Annex I route in Article 6(1) if it is a safety component of a medical device required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under Union harmonisation legislation. The Article 6(3) derogation is unlikely to apply: a system that recommends treatment regimens materially influences the outcome of clinical decision-making and does not merely perform a narrow procedural or preparatory task. As a provider of a high-risk system, the obligations across the lifecycle are as follows. Before placing the system on the market, the provider must establish, implement, document and maintain a risk management system under Article 9, identifying and analysing known and foreseeable risks to health, safety and fundamental rights, estimating risks under reasonably foreseeable misuse, and adopting targeted mitigation measures, with testing to ensure consistent performance. The provider must apply data governance under Article 10, ensuring training, validation and test datasets are relevant, sufficiently representative, and as free of errors and complete as possible, with appropriate statistical properties for the oncology population intended. Technical documentation must be drawn up under Article 11 (content governed by Annex IV), and the system must be designed for sufficient transparency to deployers under Article 13, with instructions for use covering the provider's identity, the system's intended purpose, accuracy metrics, known limitations, human oversight measures, and guidance on interpreting outputs. The system must achieve appropriate levels of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity throughout its lifecycle under Article 15, with accuracy metrics declared in the instructions for use and resilience against errors and adversarial attacks. A quality management system must be in place under Article 17. The system must undergo conformity assessment under Article 43 before market placement, and the provider must draw up an EU declaration of conformity and affix the CE marking as required by Article 16. Registration in the EU database must occur before placing the system on the market under Article 49(1). During the lifecycle, the provider must keep automatically generated logs for at least six months under Article 19, maintain post-market monitoring under Article 72, and report serious incidents under Article 73. Where a third party such as a distributor or deployer puts its own name on the system or makes a substantial modification, that party becomes a provider under Article 25(1) and assumes all provider obligations, and the original provider must cooperate and supply the necessary information and technical access under Article 25(2). Where the provider is established outside the Union, it must appoint an authorised representative in the Union by written mandate before placing the system on the market under Article 22.
```

**Branch live answer:**

```
An oncology treatment-regimen recommendation tool is high-risk under Article 6(2) read with Annex III, because recommending treatment regimens in a clinical context falls within the Annex III category covering AI systems used in health and the provision of healthcare. Before placing the system on the market, the provider must complete the conformity assessment procedure based on internal control as set out in Article 43(2), which for Annex III points 2 to 8 systems does not require a notified body, and then draw up a written, machine-readable EU declaration of conformity containing the information in Annex V under Article 47, keeping it available to national competent authorities for ten years. The provider must register itself and the system in the EU database maintained under Article 71 before placing the system on the market, as required by Article 49(1). Across the lifecycle the provider must operate a risk management system that identifies and analyses known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, estimates risks arising from reasonably foreseeable misuse, and adopts targeted mitigation measures, under Article 9. It must apply data governance and management practices to training, validation and testing datasets, ensuring those datasets are relevant, sufficiently representative and as free of errors as possible, and must examine them for biases likely to affect health and safety or fundamental rights, under Article 10. It must draw up and maintain technical documentation under Article 11, keep the automatically generated logs for at least six months under Article 19, and operate a quality management system covering regulatory-compliance strategy, design verification, testing procedures, post-market monitoring and incident-reporting workflows under Article 17. Where any distributor, importer, deployer or other third party affixes its name or trademark to the system, makes a substantial modification, or modifies the intended purpose so that the system becomes or remains high-risk, that party becomes a provider and assumes all the obligations above under Article 25(1). The provider and any third-party supplier of AI systems, tools, services, components or processes integrated into the high-risk system must specify by written agreement the information, capabilities, technical access and other assistance needed for the provider to comply with its obligations, under Article 25(4), unless the third party makes those components available under a free and open-source licence. If the underlying model is a general-purpose AI model, its provider separately bears the Article 53 obligations: technical documentation per Annex XI, downstream-provider information per Annex XII, a copyright compliance policy, and a publicly available training-data summary. Where cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 floating-point operations, the model is presumed to have systemic risk under Article 51(2) and additional systemic-risk obligations apply under Article 55.
```

### medtech:grb_07 (row 54/84)

- **gold refs**: Article 26, Article 27
- **base refs**: Article 26, Article 27, Article 13, Article 86, Article 79.1  (gold_dropped=0, loose=1.000)
- **branch refs**: Article 26, Article 27, Article 13, Article 86, Article 79.1  (gold_dropped=0, loose=1.000)

**Base live answer:**

```
A hospital deploying a high-risk AI diagnostic system carries four principal obligations as a deployer. First, under Article 26, the deployer must take appropriate technical and organisational measures to use the system in accordance with the instructions for use, assign human oversight to competent and trained natural persons, monitor the system's operation on the basis of those instructions, and retain the automatically generated logs for at least six months. Where the deployer has reason to consider that use of the system may present a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), it must without undue delay inform the provider or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authority, and suspend use. Where a serious incident is identified, the deployer must immediately inform the provider and then the importer or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authorities. Second, under Article 27, a deployer that is a body governed by public law or a private entity providing public services must perform a fundamental rights impact assessment before first use, covering the deployment processes, the period and frequency of use, the categories of persons likely to be affected, the specific risks of harm to those persons, the implementation of human oversight measures, and the measures to be taken if those risks materialise. The deployer must then notify the market surveillance authority of the results. Third, Article 13 places a design obligation on the provider to supply instructions for use that are sufficiently transparent to enable the deployer to interpret the system's output and use it appropriately; the deployer must use that information to discharge its own obligations, including, where applicable, a data protection impact assessment under the General Data Protection Regulation. Fourth, under Article 86, any person subject to a decision taken by the deployer on the basis of the system's output that produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects that person adversely in terms of health, safety or fundamental rights has the right to obtain from the deployer a clear and meaningful explanation of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken, unless an exception under Union or national law applies or that right is already provided for under other Union law.
```

**Branch live answer:**

A hospital deploying a high-risk AI diagnostic system carries four principal obligations as a deployer. First, under Article 26, the deployer must use the system in accordance with the instructions for use, assign human oversight to competent and trained natural persons, monitor the system's operation on the basis of those instructions, and retain the automatically generated logs for at least six months. Where the deployer has reason to consider that use of the system may present a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), it must without undue delay inform the provider or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authority, and suspend use. Where a serious incident is identified, the deployer must immediately inform the provider and then the importer or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authorities. Second, under Article 27, a deployer that is a body governed by public law or a private entity providing public services must, before first use, perform a fundamental rights impact assessment covering the deployment processes, the period and frequency of use, the categories of persons likely to be affected, the specific risks of harm to those persons, the implementation of human oversight measures, and the measures to be taken if those risks materialise. The deployer must notify the market surveillance authority of the results. A hospital that is a public body or provides public services falls within this obligation; one that does not falls outside it. Third, Article 13 places a design obligation on the provider to supply instructions for use that are sufficiently transparent to enable the deployer to interpret the system's output and use it appropriately, including information on capabilities, limitations, accuracy metrics, and human oversight measures. The deployer must draw on that information to discharge its Article 26 monitoring and oversight duties. Fourth, under Article 86, any person subject to a decision taken by the deployer on the basis of the system's output that produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects that person adversely in terms of health, safety or fundamental rights has the right to obtain from the deployer a clear and meaningful explanation of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken.
```

### expert_review:xr_10 (row 55/84)

- **base refs**: Article 3, Article 25, Article 16, Article 26  (gold_dropped=0, loose=1.000)
- **branch refs**: Article 3, Article 25, Article 16, Article 26  (gold_dropped=0, loose=1.000)

**Base live answer:**

```
A provider (Article 3(3)) develops an AI system, or has one developed, and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name or trademark. A deployer (Article 3(4)) uses an AI system under its authority in the course of a professional activity, so the provider bears the design and conformity duties of Article 16 while the deployer bears the use-phase duties of Article 26. Under Article 25 a deployer, distributor, importer, or other third party becomes a provider, and assumes the Article 16 provider obligations, where it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already on the market, makes a substantial modification to such a system, or modifies a system's intended purpose so that it becomes high-risk.
```

### graphrag:med_6 (row 56/84)

- **gold refs**: Article 6, Annex III
- **base refs**: Article 6.1, Article 50.1, Annex III, Annex I  (gold_dropped=0, loose=1.000)
- **branch refs**: Annex III, Annex I, Article 6, Article 50.1  (gold_dropped=0, loose=1.000)

**Base live answer:**

```
Not high-risk under ordinary circumstances. An AI system used solely to schedule administrative appointments in a clinic does not fall within any of the Annex III use cases and is not a safety component of a product requiring third-party conformity assessment under the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, so neither route under Article 6 is satisfied. It is high-risk only where the scheduling function is embedded in or constitutes a safety component of a regulated medical device that must undergo third-party conformity assessment under Annex I legislation, in which case Article 6(1) would apply. Where the system interacts directly with natural persons, the provider must ensure those persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system under Article 50(1).
```

**Base live answer:**

```
Article 10 is the operative provision. Training, validation and testing datasets must be subject to data governance and management practices appropriate for the intended purpose, covering the relevant design choices, data collection processes and the origin of data, relevant data preparation operations such as annotation, labelling, cleaning, updating, enrichment and aggregation, the formulation of assumptions about what the data measures, an assessment of the availability, quantity and suitability of the datasets needed, examination for possible biases likely to affect health and safety or to have a negative impact on fundamental rights or lead to discrimination, appropriate measures to detect, prevent and mitigate those biases, and the identification of relevant data gaps or shortcomings and how they can be addressed (Article 10(2)). The datasets must be relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose, with appropriate statistical properties as regards the persons or groups of persons in relation to whom the system is intended to be used (Article 10(3)). They must also take into account, to the extent required by the intended purpose, the characteristics or elements particular to the specific geographical, contextual, behavioural or functional setting in which the system is intended to be used (Article 10(4)), and where a system trained and tested on data reflecting that specific setting is presumed to comply with Article 10(4), that presumption of conformity applies (Article 42(1)). To the extent strictly necessary for bias detection and correction, the provider may process special categories of personal data (Article 10(5)). The technical documentation drawn up before the system is placed on the market must include datasheets describing the training methodologies and techniques, the training datasets used, their provenance, scope and main characteristics, how the data was obtained and selected, labelling procedures and data cleaning methodologies (Article 11, Annex IV).
```

### graphrag:ng_01 (row 59/84)

- **gold refs**: Article 7, Article 9
- **base refs**: Article 7.2, Article 9, Annex III  (gold_dropped=0, loose=1.000)
- **branch refs**: Article 7.2, Article 9, Article 6  (gold_dropped=0, loose=1.000)

**Base live answer:**

```
The Regulation supplies two distinct sets of criteria: one for classifying whether a use case belongs in the high-risk category, and one for managing risk once a system is classified as high-risk. For classification purposes, Article 7(2) lists the criteria the Commission must apply when assessing whether an AI use case poses a significant risk of harm sufficient to warrant inclusion in, or removal from, the Annex III list: the intended purpose of the system; the extent to which it has been or is likely to be used; the nature and amount of data processed, including whether special categories of personal data are involved; the degree of autonomy and the possibility for a human to override potentially harmful decisions or recommendations; whether use of the system has already caused harm to health, safety or fundamental rights or given rise to significant concerns; the potential extent and intensity of harm, including whether it could affect multiple persons or disproportionately affect a particular group; the degree to which affected persons are dependent on the outcome and cannot reasonably opt out; the existence of a power imbalance or vulnerability between affected persons and the deployer; whether the outcome is easily corrigible or reversible, with adverse impacts on health, safety or fundamental rights not considered easily corrigible; the magnitude and likelihood of benefit to individuals, groups or society; and the extent to which existing Union law provides effective redress or prevention measures. For ongoing risk management of a high-risk system, Article 9 requires a continuous iterative process across the system's entire lifecycle comprising: identification and analysis of known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety or fundamental rights when the system is used for its intended purpose; estimation and evaluation of risks arising under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse; evaluation of risks arising from post-market monitoring data; and adoption of appropriate and targeted risk management measures, with residual risks judged acceptable and communicated to the deployer.
```

**Branch live answer:**

```
The Regulation supplies two distinct sets of risk-assessment criteria depending on the question being asked. For classifying a system as high-risk in the first place, Article 6 provides the operative framework: a system is high-risk either because it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by Annex I harmonisation legislation that requires third-party conformity assessment, or because it falls within one of the use cases listed in Annex III. For deciding whether to add, modify or remove use cases from Annex III by delegated act, Article 7(2) sets out the criteria the Commission must apply: the intended purpose of the AI system; the extent to which it has been or is likely to be used; the nature and amount of data processed, including whether special categories of personal data are involved; the degree of autonomy and the possibility for a human to override potentially harmful outputs; whether the system has already caused harm to health, safety or fundamental rights or given rise to significant concerns; the potential extent and intensity of such harm, including whether it could affect multiple persons or disproportionately affect a particular group; the degree to which affected persons are dependent on the outcome and cannot reasonably opt out; the existence of a power imbalance or vulnerability of those potentially harmed; whether the outcome is easily corrigible or reversible; the magnitude and likelihood of benefit to individuals, groups or society; and the extent to which existing Union law provides effective redress or prevention measures. For ongoing risk assessment of a high-risk system already in use, Article 9 requires a continuous iterative risk management system covering identification and analysis of known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, estimation and evaluation of risks arising from intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse, evaluation of risks emerging from post-market monitoring data, and adoption of targeted mitigation and control measures, with residual risks judged acceptable.

### medtech:grb_17 (row 60/84)

- **gold refs**: Article 50
- **base refs**: Article 6.1, Annex III, Annex I  (gold_dropped=1, loose=0.000)
- **branch refs**: Article 6.1, Article 49.2, Annex I  (gold_dropped=1, loose=0.000)

**Base live answer:**

```
Not high-risk on the facts stated, though the classification is conditional. An ambient scribe that only transcribes doctor-patient consultations does not fall within any of the eight Annex III use cases, and the question does not indicate it is a safety component of, or itself a product requiring third-party conformity assessment under, the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I. Neither route under Article 6 is satisfied. The system is therefore minimal risk, carrying no Chapter III Section 2 obligations. The classification would change if the system were placed on the market as, or integrated as a safety component into, a medical device required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under the medical devices regulation listed in Annex I, in which case Article 6(1) would make it high-risk. It would also change if the intended purpose were expanded to include emotion recognition, biometric categorisation, or any other Annex III use case, which would engage Article 6(2).
```

**Branch live answer:**

```
Explicitly not high-risk, subject to one qualifying condition. An AI ambient scribe whose sole function is transcribing doctor-patient consultations performs a narrow procedural task and does not materially influence the outcome of decision making, so the Article 6(3) derogation applies and the system falls outside the high-risk tier despite the medical context. The provider must nonetheless document that assessment before placing the system on the market and register the system in the EU database under Article 49(2). If the system were instead classified or used as a safety component of a medical device required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, the Article 6(1) route would make it high-risk, but a pure transcription function does not satisfy that condition.
```

**Base live answer:**

```
The deploying hospital, as a deployer, must retain the logs automatically generated by the high-risk radiology system for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the system, and in any event for at least six months, unless applicable Union or national law (including Union law on the protection of personal data) requires a different period, as Article 26(6) states. That retention duty applies to the extent the logs are under the deployer's control. Article 12(1) requires the system itself to be technically capable of automatically recording events over its lifetime, and Article 12(2) specifies that the logging capabilities must enable recording of events relevant to identifying risk situations, facilitating post-market monitoring, and monitoring the operation of the system. The provider, separately, must also keep those automatically generated logs for at least six months under Article 19, and must retain the technical documentation, quality management system documentation, any notified-body documents, and the EU declaration of conformity for ten years after the system is placed on the market or put into service under Article 18.
```

**Branch live answer:**

```
The provider must design the system to record events automatically over its lifetime, with logging capabilities that capture events relevant to identifying risks, facilitating post-market monitoring, and monitoring operation (Article 12(1) and Article 12(2)). The provider keeps those automatically generated logs for a period appropriate to the intended purpose, at a minimum of six months, unless Union or national law requires otherwise (Article 19). The deploying hospital, as deployer, independently must keep the logs automatically generated by the system to the extent such logs are under its control, again for a period appropriate to the intended purpose and at least six months, unless Union or national law provides otherwise (Article 26(6)). Where a competent authority makes a reasoned request, the provider must also give that authority access to the automatically generated logs to the extent they are under the provider's control, and any information so obtained is subject to confidentiality obligations (Article 21).
```

The conformity assessment route is the one prescribed by Article 43(3): the provider follows the relevant conformity assessment procedure required under the applicable sectoral legislation, the Chapter III Section 2 requirements form part of that assessment, and the notified body already notified under the sectoral legislation is entitled to control conformity with those requirements. - **branch refs**: Article 14, Article 13.3.d, Article 26.2  (gold_dropped=0, loose=1.000)

**Base live answer:**

```
Article 14 is the operative provision. The provider must design the system so that the natural persons assigned to oversight can properly understand the system's capacities and limitations and duly monitor its operation, including by detecting anomalies, dysfunctions and unexpected performance (Article 14(4)(a)). Those persons must remain aware of the possible tendency to automatically rely or over-rely on the system's output, that is, automation bias, which is particularly relevant for a system used to provide information or recommendations for decisions taken by natural persons (Article 14(4)(b)). They must be able to correctly interpret the system's output, taking into account interpretation tools and methods available (Article 14(4)(c)). They must be able to decide, in any particular situation, not to use the system or to disregard, override or reverse its output (Article 14(4)(d)), and to intervene in or interrupt the system's operation through a stop button or similar procedure that allows the system to come to a halt in a safe state (Article 14(4)(e)). On the deployer side, Article 26(2) requires the deployer to assign that oversight to natural persons who have the necessary competence, training and authority, as well as the necessary support, and Article 26(1) requires the deployer to use the system in accordance with the instructions for use. Those instructions must themselves describe the human oversight measures and the technical measures put in place to facilitate interpretation of the system's outputs, as Article 13(3)(d) requires of the provider.
```

**Branch live answer:**

```
Article 14 is the operative provision. The provider must design and develop the system so that the natural persons assigned to oversight are enabled to properly understand the system's capacities and limitations and duly monitor its operation, including detecting anomalies and dysfunctions (Article 14(4)(a)); to remain aware of the possible tendency to automatically rely or over-rely on the system's output, that is, automation bias (Article 14(4)(b)); to correctly interpret the system's output (Article 14(4)(c)); to decide, in any particular situation, not to use the system or to disregard, override or reverse its output (Article 14(4)(d)); and to intervene in or interrupt the system through a stop button or similar procedure that allows it to halt in a safe state (Article 14(4)(e)). These measures must be commensurate with the risks, level of autonomy and context of use, and may be built into the system by the provider, identified by the provider for implementation by the deployer, or both (Article 14(3)). On the deployer side, Article 26(2) requires the deployer to assign human oversight to natural persons who have the necessary competence, training and authority, as well as the necessary support. The provider must also supply instructions for use that describe the human oversight measures and any technical tools available to help the deployer interpret the system's output (Article 13(3)(d)).
```

### graphrag:gt_03 (row 67/84)

- **gold refs**: Article 6
- **base refs**: Article 6, Annex I, Annex III  (gold_dropped=0, loose=1.000)
- **branch refs**: Article 6, Article 49.2, Annex I  (gold_dropped=0, loose=1.000)

**Base live answer:**

```
An AI system is high-risk under Article 6 on two distinct routes. Under Article 6(1), the system is high-risk where two cumulative conditions are met: the system is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. Under Article 6(2), a system is high-risk where it falls within one of the use case categories listed in Annex III, which covers biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, access to essential private and public services and benefits, law enforcement, migration and asylum and border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes. Article 6(3) provides a derogation from the Annex III route: an Annex III system is not high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making, and where it performs only a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns or deviations from prior patterns without replacing or influencing the previously completed human assessment, or performs a preparatory task. That derogation does not apply where the system performs profiling of natural persons, in which case it is always high-risk regardless of the other conditions.
```

**Branch live answer:**

```
An AI system is high-risk under two separate routes established by Article 6. The first route, under Article 6(1), applies where the system is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. Both conditions must be satisfied. The second route, under Article 6(2), applies where the system falls within one of the use-case categories listed in Annex III, which covers biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, access to essential private and public services and benefits, law enforcement, migration and asylum and border control, and the administration of justice and democratic processes. An Annex III system escapes high-risk classification under Article 6(3) where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, and where it performs only a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the previously completed human assessment, or performs a preparatory task. A system that performs profiling of natural persons is always high-risk regardless of those conditions. A provider relying on this derogation must document its assessment before placing the system on the market and must register under Article 49(2).
```

### graphrag:med_02 (row 69/84)

- **gold refs**: Article 5, Article 6, Annex III
- **base refs**: Article 5.1.g, Article 6.2, Article 6.1, Annex III.1.b, Annex I  (gold_dropped=0, loose=1.000)
- **branch refs**: Article 5.1.g, Article 6.2, Annex III.1.b, Annex III.1  (gold_dropped=0, loose=1.000)

**Base live answer:**

```
Likely high-risk, with one conditional prohibition to assess first. Where the system uses biometric data to deduce or infer race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life, or sexual orientation as part of the sorting process, it is a prohibited biometric categorisation system under Article 5(1)(g), regardless of the clinical trial context. Absent that prohibited dimension, sorting patients by biometric data to determine priority for a clinical trial is high-risk under Article 6(2) where the system performs biometric categorisation according to sensitive or protected attributes or characteristics based on the inference of those attributes or characteristics, which is the use case listed in Annex III(1)(b). Where the system instead uses biometric data solely for identity verification, confirming that a specific natural person is who they claim to be, it falls outside that Annex III listing and is not high-risk on that route; it may still be high-risk under Article 6(1) if it is a safety component of, or is itself, a medical device required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I. The deciding facts are therefore whether the biometric sorting infers sensitive or protected attributes, and, if not, whether the product requires third-party conformity assessment under Annex I legislation.
```

**Branch live answer:**

```
Likely high-risk, with one conditional prohibition to assess first. Where the system uses biometric data to deduce or infer race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life, or sexual orientation as part of the sorting process, it is a prohibited biometric categorisation system under Article 5(1)(g), regardless of the clinical-trial context. Where the system does not infer those sensitive attributes, it is high-risk under Article 6(2) as a biometric categorisation system according to sensitive or protected attributes or characteristics based on the inference of those attributes or characteristics, which is the use case listed in Annex III(1)(b); the deciding condition is whether the biometric data is used to assign patients to categories based on such attributes. A system that sorts patients purely on clinically neutral biometric parameters without inferring any of the Article 5(1)(g) attributes falls outside the prohibition but remains high-risk under Article 6(2) read with Annex III(1)(b), provided the use of biometrics for that purpose is permitted under relevant Union or national law as Annex III(1) requires.
```

### graphrag:gt_04 (row 71/84)

- **gold refs**: Article 6
- **base refs**: Article 6.3, Annex III, Annex I  (gold_dropped=0, loose=1.000)
- **branch refs**: Article 6.3, Annex III, Annex I  (gold_dropped=0, loose=1.000)

**Base live answer:**

```
An AI system is high-risk under Article 6 on either of two routes: it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation, or it falls within one of the eight use-case categories listed in Annex III. Those eight Annex III categories are: biometrics (remote biometric identification systems, biometric categorisation systems inferring sensitive or protected attributes, and emotion recognition systems); critical infrastructure (safety components in the management and operation of critical digital infrastructure, road traffic, or the supply of water, gas, heating or electricity); education and vocational training; employment, workers management and access to self-employment (recruitment and selection, decisions on terms of work, promotion, termination, task allocation based on individual behaviour or personal traits, and performance monitoring); essential private and public services; law enforcement; migration, asylum and border control management; and administration of justice and democratic processes. An Annex III system escapes high-risk classification under Article 6(3) where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights and performs only a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns without replacing or influencing the prior human assessment, or performs a preparatory task. A system that performs profiling of natural persons is always high-risk regardless of those conditions, and a provider relying on the derogation must document its assessment before placing the system on the market.
```

**Branch live answer:**

```
A system is high-risk under the Regulation on two distinct routes, both set out in Article 6. The first route applies where the system is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. Annex I covers products such as machinery, toys, radio equipment, medical devices, in vitro diagnostic medical devices, lifts, pressure equipment, personal protective equipment, gas appliances, recreational craft, cableway installations, civil aviation security equipment, and agricultural and forestry vehicles. The second route applies where the system falls within one of the eight use-case categories listed in Annex III: biometrics (including remote biometric identification systems, biometric categorisation according to sensitive or protected attributes, and emotion recognition); critical infrastructure (safety components in the management of critical digital infrastructure, road traffic, or the supply of water, gas, heating or electricity); education and vocational training; employment, workers management and access to self-employment (recruitment, task allocation, performance monitoring, promotion and termination decisions); essential private and public services; law enforcement; migration, asylum and border control management; and administration of justice and democratic processes. An Annex III system escapes high-risk classification under Article 6(3) only where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, and performs one of four tasks: a narrow procedural task, improving the result of a previously completed human activity, detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the prior human assessment, or a preparatory task. A system that performs profiling of natural persons is always high-risk regardless of those conditions, and a provider relying on the derogation must document its assessment before placing the system on the market and register under Article 49(2).
```

### graphrag:ng_05 (row 73/84)

- **gold refs**: Article 11, Article 13, Article 18, Article 21, Article 23
- **base refs**: Annex IV, Article 11, Article 13  (gold_dropped=3, loose=0.400)
- **branch refs**: Annex IV, Article 21, Article 13, Article 18, Article 11  (gold_dropped=1, loose=0.800)

**Base live answer:**

```
The provider of a high-risk AI system must draw up technical documentation before placing the system on the market, keep it up to date, and ensure it demonstrates conformity with the applicable requirements; the minimum content is set out in Annex IV, covering system description and design specifications, system architecture and computational resources, data and training methodology, human oversight measures, validation and testing procedures, cybersecurity measures, the risk management system, and a copy of the EU declaration of conformity (Article 11). The system must also be designed and developed so that its operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret its output and use it appropriately, supported by instructions for use that identify the provider, describe the system's capabilities and limitations including accuracy and robustness metrics, flag known or foreseeable circumstances that may lead to risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, describe human oversight measures, and specify computational and hardware resources and maintenance requirements (Article 13). The provider must retain the technical documentation, quality management system documentation, any notified body decisions, and the EU declaration of conformity for ten years after the system is placed on the market and make them available to national competent authorities on request (Article 18). Upon a reasoned request from a competent authority, the provider must supply all information and documentation necessary to demonstrate conformity, in an official Union language, and that information is subject to confidentiality obligations (Article 21).
```

**Branch live answer:**

```
A provider of a high-risk AI system must draw up technical documentation before placing the system on the market, keep it up to date, and ensure it contains at minimum the elements set out in Annex IV, which covers system description, design specifications, architecture, data and training methodology, human oversight measures, risk management measures, and validation and testing procedures (Article 11). The system must also be designed so that its operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret its output and use it appropriately, supported by instructions for use that identify the provider, describe the system's intended purpose, capabilities, limitations, accuracy metrics, known risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, human oversight measures, and computational and hardware requirements (Article 13). The provider must keep the technical documentation, quality management system documentation, any notified body approvals, and the EU declaration of conformity at the disposal of national competent authorities for ten years after the system is placed on the market (Article 18). Upon a reasoned request from a competent authority, the provider must supply all information and documentation necessary to demonstrate conformity with the Section 2 requirements, in an official Union language, and any information so provided is treated as confidential in accordance with obligations protecting intellectual property rights, trade secrets and source code (Article 21, Article 78). Where the provider is established outside the Union, a written mandate must empower an authorised representative to verify that the declaration of conformity and technical documentation were drawn up, to keep them available for ten years, and to supply them to competent authorities on request (Article 22).
```

### graphrag:ng_06 (row 74/84) 🚫

- **gold refs**: Article 43, Annex VI, Annex VII
- **base refs**: Article 43.4, Annex VI, Annex VII  (gold_dropped=0, loose=1.000)
- **branch refs**: Article 43.2, Article 43.4, Article 17  (gold_dropped=2, loose=0.333)

**Base live answer:**

```
A conformity assessment for a high-risk AI system follows one of two procedures depending on the system's Annex III category and whether harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied. For systems listed in point 1 of Annex III, the provider may choose the internal control procedure under Annex VI where harmonised standards or common specifications are applied; that procedure requires the provider to verify that the quality management system conforms to the relevant requirements, examine the technical documentation for compliance with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, and verify that the design and development process and the post-market monitoring plan are consistent with that documentation, all without notified body involvement. Where harmonised standards do not exist, are not fully applied, or are published with a restriction, the provider must instead follow the notified body procedure under Annex VII, under which a notified body audits the quality management system against the same requirements, examines the technical documentation, issues an EU technical documentation assessment certificate, and carries out periodic surveillance audits. For systems listed in points 2 to 8 of Annex III, the provider follows only the internal control procedure under Annex VI, with no notified body involvement regardless of whether harmonised standards are applied. A substantial modification to a system that has already undergone conformity assessment requires a new conformity assessment procedure under Article 43(4), except that pre-determined post-market changes documented in the technical documentation at the time of initial assessment do not constitute a substantial modification.
```

**Branch live answer:**

```
A conformity assessment for a high-risk AI system follows one of two procedures depending on the system's Annex III category and whether harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied. For systems listed in point 1 of Annex III, the provider may choose the internal control procedure set out in Annex VI, under which the provider itself verifies that its quality management system complies with Article 17, examines the technical documentation to assess compliance with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, and verifies that the design, development and post-market monitoring process is consistent with that documentation, all without notified body involvement. Where harmonised standards do not exist, have not been applied in full, or have been published with a restriction, the provider must instead follow the procedure in Annex VII, under which a notified body audits the quality management system against Article 17, examines the technical documentation, issues a Union technical documentation assessment certificate, and carries out ongoing surveillance through periodic audits. For systems listed in points 2 to 8 of Annex III, Article 43(2) requires the provider to follow only the internal control procedure in Annex VI, with no notified body involvement. A system that has already undergone conformity assessment must undergo a new assessment upon any substantial modification, under Article 43(4), except that pre-determined changes to a continuously learning system that are documented in the technical documentation at the time of initial assessment do not constitute a substantial modification.
```

- **branch refs**: Article 2  (gold_dropped=0, loose=1.000)

**Base live answer:**

```
Under Article 2(6), the Regulation does not apply to AI systems or models, including their output, specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development. Article 2(8) further excludes any research, testing or development activity on AI systems prior to their being placed on the market or put into service, except testing in real-world conditions. The Act's obligations therefore attach only once the system leaves pure R&D and is placed on the market or put into service, at which point the operator's duties follow the system's risk classification.
```

### graphrag:med_03 (row 80/84) 🚫

- **gold refs**: Article 53, Article 51, Article 55
- **base refs**: Article 53.1, Article 50, Article 51.2  (gold_dropped=1, loose=0.667)
- **branch refs**: Article 53.1.a, Article 53.1, Annex XI  (gold_dropped=2, loose=0.333)

**Base live answer:**

```
As a provider of a general-purpose AI model, the startup's core transparency obligations arise under Article 53(1), which requires it to draw up and keep up-to-date technical documentation of the model including its training and testing process and evaluation results (Article 53(1)(a)), make available to downstream providers the information they need to understand the model's capabilities and limitations and to comply with their own obligations (Article 53(1)(b)), put in place a policy to comply with Union law on copyright and related rights (Article 53(1)(c)), and draw up and make publicly available a sufficiently detailed summary about the content used for training the model (Article 53(1)(d)). The obligations in Article 53(1)(a) and Article 53(1)(b) do not apply where the model is released under a free and open-source licence that permits access, use, modification and distribution and whose parameters, including weights, model architecture and usage information, are made publicly available. That carve-out does not extend to the copyright policy or the public training-data summary, which apply to all providers regardless of licence. The carve-out also falls away entirely if the model is classified as having systemic risk under Article 51. If the cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 floating-point operations, the model is presumed to have high-impact capabilities and is classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk under Article 51(2), triggering the additional obligations in Article 55(1): adversarial testing and evaluation against standardised protocols, assessment and mitigation of systemic risks at Union level, tracking and reporting serious incidents to the AI Office without undue delay, and ensuring adequate cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure. Article 50 transparency duties attach to the model only if it is integrated into a system that interacts directly with natural persons or generates synthetic content; those duties are actor-specific and the question of whether they apply depends on how the model is deployed downstream rather than on the model alone.
```

**Branch live answer:**

```
As a general-purpose AI model provider, the startup's transparency obligations under Article 53 are: technical documentation kept up to date per Annex XI (which requires a general description, architecture, training data, computational resources and energy consumption), information made available to downstream providers who intend to integrate the model into their AI systems, a copyright compliance policy, and a publicly available summary of the content used for training. The obligations in Article 53(1)(a) and (b), covering technical documentation and downstream-provider information, do not apply if the model is released under a free and open-source licence with publicly available parameters, but that carve-out falls away entirely if the model is classified as having systemic risk under Article 51. Systemic risk is presumed where cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 floating-point operations, and if that threshold is met the provider must additionally perform model evaluation including adversarial testing, assess and mitigate systemic risks at Union level, track and report serious incidents to the AI Office, and ensure adequate cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure, all under Article 55. If the model is made available in a system that interacts directly with natural persons, Article 50(1) requires the provider to design that system so natural persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system, and Article 50(2) requires synthetic outputs to be marked in a machine-readable format as artificially generated.
```

```
For high-risk AI systems the applicable penalty ceiling is set by Article 99(4): administrative fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or, for an undertaking, up to 3 % of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, for non-compliance with the obligations on providers, deployers, importers and distributors (every obligation other than the Article 5 prohibitions, which carry the higher Article 99(3) ceiling of EUR 35 000 000 or 7 %). Under Article 99(6), for SMEs and start-ups each fine is capped at the lower of the percentage or the fixed amount. Penalties must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive.
```

- **branch refs**: Article 5, Article 6, Article 50, Article 53, Annex I  (gold_dropped=1, loose=0.750)

**Base live answer:**

```
The EU AI Act applies a risk-based framework with four tiers for AI systems, plus a parallel regime for general-purpose AI models. The first tier is prohibited practices: Article 5 bans eight categories outright, including subliminal or manipulative techniques causing significant harm, exploitation of vulnerabilities, social scoring, predictive policing based solely on profiling, untargeted scraping to build facial recognition databases, emotion recognition in the workplace and education institutions except for medical or safety reasons, biometric categorisation that deduces race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation, and real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement outside three narrow objectives. The second tier is high-risk: Article 6 classifies a system as high-risk on two independent routes, first where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment, and second where it falls within one of the use-case categories listed in Annex III, which covers biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, access to essential private and public services and benefits, law enforcement, migration and border management, and administration of justice and democratic processes, subject to the derogation in Article 6(3) for systems that do not pose a significant risk of harm and perform only a narrow procedural, preparatory, pattern-detection or human-activity-improvement task, provided the system does not perform profiling of natural persons. The third tier is limited risk, carrying the Article 50 transparency obligations: providers must design systems that interact directly with natural persons so those persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system, and must mark synthetic audio, image, video or text in a machine-readable format as artificially generated or manipulated, while deployers must inform persons exposed to an emotion recognition or biometric categorisation system and disclose deepfake content. The fourth tier is minimal risk, for which the Regulation imposes no mandatory obligations. Running in parallel rather than inside these tiers, general-purpose AI models are governed by Articles 51 to 56: all such providers carry the Article 53 documentation, downstream-provider information, copyright policy and training-data summary duties, while models classified as having systemic risk under Article 51, presumed where cumulative training compute exceeds 10²⁵ floating-point operations, additionally carry the Article 55 duties of adversarial model evaluation, systemic risk assessment and mitigation, serious incident reporting, and cybersecurity protection.
```
